newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang defector sets self mission to save Korea.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang defector sets self mission to save Korea.

text.p: The tell-tale bulge of a bullet-proof vest beneath his dark suit underlined the danger of the mission Hwang Jang-yop had set himself -- to save the Korean peninsula from war.
A frail man with thinning hair and glasses, Hwang flew into South Korea on Sunday, the highest-ranked Pyongyang official ever to flee his communist homeland.
North Korea, he declared, had turned its back on reform and was bent on conflict.
"North Korea denounces reform and opening as an unsocialist path. It is only seeking a confrontation of military power while rejecting dialogue with South Korea," he said.

"Confrontation between North and South today is not a confrontation between socialism and capitalism. It is a confrontation between feudal dictatorship and free democracy, a confrontation between feudal militarism and a capitalistic economy, a confrontation between war and peace."

The chief architect of North Korea's guiding ideology of "juche", or self-reliance, should know. As a former confidante of leader Kim Jong-il, he holds the innermost secrets of the world's most tightly-sealed society.
Yet the surprise presented by Hwang at a Seoul military air base was not so much the message as the messenger.

Pyongyang does little to mask its warlike posture, and despite famine and economic collapse there have been few signs North Korea is ready to copy socialist neighbour China and adopt market-style changes.
The real shock was that Hwang had turned up in person on a self-proclaimed crusade to strive for peaceful reunification of the two Koreas.
Some have suggested Hwang's betrayal of a system he constructed would be akin to Lenin fleeing Russia, or Karl Marx denouncing class struggle.

They see his defection as an indication that the world's last Stalinist outpost is crumbling -- a prospect, ironically, that fills South Korea and the United States with alarm after decades of Cold War rivalry.
The fear is that as it faces the prospect of its own destruction, the North Korean leadership will decide it has nothing to lose by unleashing military terror.
A 1.1 million-strong army, some 10,000 artillery pieces pointed at Seoul, chemical and possibly biological weapons are almost all Pyongyang has to show for its socialist endeavours.
"North Korea seems to think there is no option but to use the powerful military force it has built up over decades," Hwang said in a statement on arrival.
His ominous words highlighted the high-stakes efforts the United States and South Korea are making to lure North Korea into accepting their offer of four-nation peace talks, also including China.

North Korean diplomats on Saturday failed for the second day to turn up at a meeting in New York scheduled to hear Pyongyang's response to the offer of talks to close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War.
The war ended with a now-fraying armistice.
There were some hopes a meeting could be rearranged for Monday, but analysts in Seoul were pessimistic about long-term prospects.
"A peace treaty with South Korea will require a huge policy change in North Korea," said Park Hun-ok, fellow at the Institute of North Korea Studies.
"South Korea has always been a target for Pyongyang's communist revolution and a peace treay will destroy the basis of its important policies."
"As North Korea is desperate for food, it will probably not walk away from peace talks but it would be naive to expect quick progress in the talks," Park said.
Lee Jong-seok, research fellow at the independent Sejong Institute, said he did not expect a peace treaty to be signed even if North Korea sat down at talks.
"It would take long time -- if ever -- for the North to agree to implement the goal of peace talks," he said.
